Worked example

A worked example illustrates handling a request from a family member. A family member of a resident at Riverside House asks to see 'everything you have' about their relative. The Data Protection Lead first confirms the family member holds a registered Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare before proceeding as a SAR on the resident's behalf; where no such authority is confirmed, the request is explained sensitively as not meeting the SAR access criteria, while still discussing what more limited information can appropriately be shared as part of ordinary care communication.

Frequently asked questions

**Does a SAR have to be made in writing?** No — a verbal request is equally valid and starts the same one-month timescale from when it is made, which is why any member of staff receiving one, however informally, must forward it immediately rather than waiting for something written. **Can Alderbridge charge a fee for a SAR?** Only in narrow circumstances (a manifestly excessive or repeat request), and never as a routine practice. **What if the requester wants only specific information, not everything held?** The response can be scoped to what they have actually asked for, agreed with them directly, rather than always providing every piece of data regardless of what was actually requested. **Can a former employee make a SAR?** Yes, without any time limit tied to when their employment ended, for as long as Alderbridge still holds personal data about them.

Verbal SARs made during a heated conversation

Where a verbal SAR is made during an otherwise heated or emotional conversation (for example, during a complaint discussion), it is still treated as a valid, timescale-triggering request, and the member of staff present notes down as much detail as they reasonably can (who, roughly what was asked, when) before forwarding it, rather than the request being lost or forgotten simply because it arose in a difficult conversational context rather than a calm, deliberate one.

Proportionate search effort for a large or long-standing record

For a data subject with a very long history at Alderbridge, the search for relevant records is still comprehensive, but the Data Protection Lead may agree a reasonable, transparent approach with the requester about how older or less central material (for example, historic rota records mentioning them only incidentally) is handled, rather than treating every search as requiring literally infinite effort regardless of the genuine relevance of what might be found, provided this is discussed openly with the requester rather than decided unilaterally to save effort.

SARs made in the context of active litigation or a legal claim

Where a SAR arrives after Alderbridge is already aware of a genuine, active legal claim or dispute involving the same individual, the Data Protection Lead may take legal advice on how the SAR and any litigation-specific disclosure rules interact, but this consultation does not itself justify missing the standard statutory timescale merely because litigation is also under way; a genuine, narrow legal exemption is applied only where it actually exists and is documented, not used as a general reason for caution or delay.

Subject Access Request (SAR) Handling Procedure

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group responds to a subject access request (SAR) — a request from a data subject to see the personal data held about them — under the UK GDPR. It applies to any SAR received about a person supported, a current or former employee, or anyone else whose personal data Alderbridge holds.

Policy statement

Alderbridge treats a subject access request as a genuine legal right the requester is exercising, not an administrative inconvenience to be managed reluctantly, and aims to respond helpfully and within the statutory timescale in every case, escalating only where a request is genuinely complex or unclear rather than defaulting to caution as a way of buying time.

Definitions

**Subject access request (SAR)** a request by a data subject (or someone with valid authority to act for them) to see the personal data held about them. **Third-party data** personal data about someone other than the requester contained within the same record, which is redacted before disclosure unless that third party consents. **Complex request** a SAR involving a particularly large volume of data or multiple systems, extending the standard response timescale. **Valid authority** the legal basis (for example, a Lasting Power of Attorney, or the data subject's own written consent) required before Alderbridge discloses personal data to someone other than the data subject themselves.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any member of staff** receiving what might be a SAR, however informally phrased, forwards it to the Data Protection Lead the same day, rather than attempting to gather the information themselves. **The Data Protection Lead** confirms the requester's identity and any authority claimed, coordinates gathering the relevant records across every system that might hold them, and completes any necessary redaction before disclosure. **Each registered manager and HR** supports the Data Protection Lead by identifying and providing the records held at their own site or function promptly when asked.

Frequently asked questions

**Can I look up a friend's relative's records if they ask me to check on their care?** No — this is exactly the
curiosity-access scenario this policy prohibits; direct them to the person's own registered manager instead.
**Is it a breach if a resident's name is visible on a whiteboard in the staff area?** It depends on who can
see the whiteboard; a staff-only area used for handover is generally acceptable, but a whiteboard visible to
visitors or other residents is not, and site managers are expected to check this specifically as part of their
own local review. **Can a family member request to see a deceased relative's records?** The right of
access under UK GDPR belongs to living individuals; a request about a deceased person is handled
differently and is referred to the Data Protection Lead rather than treated as an ordinary subject access
request. **What if I accidentally send a text message containing a resident's name to the wrong number?**
Report it the same way as any other suspected breach, however small it feels — the Data Protection Lead,
not the individual member of staff, decides whether it is significant enough to escalate further.

Training and competency

All staff complete information governance training at induction and annually thereafter, per the Mandatory
Training Matrix, including specific modules on subject access requests and recognising a data breach. The
Data Protection Lead additionally completes a more advanced, externally accredited data protection
qualification.

A final practical reminder for every member of staff

You do not need to know the details of this whole procedure to do the one thing that matters most: if someone asks what personal data Alderbridge holds about them, tell the Data Protection Lead the same day, and let the rest of this procedure do its job from there — you do not need to assess authority, redaction, or timescale yourself; that is precisely what the Data Protection Lead exists to do once told, and doing so promptly is the single most useful contribution any individual member of staff can make to this whole procedure working as intended, more useful by far than trying to assess the request's validity or scope yourself before passing it on, since that assessment genuinely requires the Data Protection Lead's own specific training and judgement, built up through handling many such requests across every part of the organisation over time, in a way a well-intentioned but untrained colleague simply could not reliably replicate on a single isolated occasion, however carefully and conscientiously they genuinely tried to help with the very best of intentions.

Extended worked example: a SAR received during active safeguarding involvement

A worked example illustrates a genuinely difficult overlap. A resident's family member submits a SAR while a safeguarding investigation involving that same family member is ongoing. The Data Protection Lead processes the SAR on its own terms and timescale, but consults the Safeguarding Lead before disclosure to check whether any specific content would compromise the ongoing safeguarding process if disclosed at this point — a narrow, evidence-based exemption that may justify withholding a specific limited element temporarily, explained to the requester as far as possible, rather than either ignoring the safeguarding context entirely or using it as a blanket reason to delay the whole SAR response beyond its statutory timescale.

Quality checking a response before it is sent

Before any SAR response is sent, a second person (not the person who prepared it) reviews it specifically for redaction completeness and factual accuracy, since a redaction mistake in a SAR response is itself a personal data breach under the Personal Data Breach Procedure, and this second check is a control specifically designed to prevent that particular failure mode.

Requests about a child in a family member's care

Occasionally a SAR-like request concerns a child rather than an adult data subject — for example, where a resident's grandchild's details appear in a visiting log; a request made on a child's behalf by a parent is assessed for the parent's own valid authority in the same way as any other third-party request, and the Data Protection Lead seeks specialist advice where the request's scope or the family circumstances are genuinely unclear.

Where a data subject has been supported or employed at more than one Alderbridge site over time, the Data Protection Lead coordinates a single search across every relevant site and system rather than each site separately deciding what falls within scope, ensuring the eventual response is genuinely complete rather than reflecting only the most recent or most obvious location.

Extended frequently asked questions

**What if some of the requested data is held by a third-party data processor (for example, a payroll provider) rather than Alderbridge directly?** The Data Protection Lead requests the relevant data from that processor under the existing data processing agreement, since the data remains Alderbridge's own responsibility to disclose regardless of where it is technically stored. **Can a SAR be refused outright?** Only in narrow, specific circumstances set out in law (for example, where an exemption genuinely applies); a request is never simply refused because it is inconvenient or time-consuming to fulfil. **How is a SAR different from an ordinary request to update incorrect information?** The latter is a rectification request, handled under a related but distinct right; the Data Protection Lead confirms which right is actually being exercised and responds accordingly, since the two have different substantive requirements even though they are related.

Redaction in practice

Redacting third-party data is not simply blacking out a name; the Data Protection Lead considers whether the surrounding context would still make the third party identifiable even with their name removed (for example, 'the resident in the next room' in a small care home), and redacts or generalises accordingly, since a technically redacted but still practically identifying disclosure does not meet this procedure's own standard.

Handling a request that appears to be motivated by an unrelated dispute

Where a SAR appears to be made in the context of a separate dispute (for example, a family disagreement, or an ongoing complaint), it is still handled exactly as any other SAR would be, in full and within the same timescale, since the requester's motivation for exercising their legal right does not change the right itself or Alderbridge's obligation to respond to it properly.

Lawful basis for key processing activities

Care record processing relies primarily on the lawful basis of vital interests and the performance of a task
carried out in the substantial public interest for special category health data, alongside the person's own
consent where they are able to give it meaningfully. Employment record processing relies on the
performance of the employment contract and compliance with legal obligations. CCTV footage relies on
legitimate interests in the safety and security of people supported, staff and visitors, as set out in the CCTV
Policy. Marketing communications, where they occur at all, rely on explicit consent, never legitimate
interests, and that consent can be withdrawn at any time.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Personal data may be shared without the data subject's consent, or even without their knowledge in a
genuine emergency, where doing so is necessary to protect someone's vital interests — for example,
sharing a resident's allergy information with a paramedic during a medical emergency — but this exception
is used narrowly, for the specific emergency at hand, never as a general licence to share more broadly.

asking a straightforward question — what do you know about me — and this procedure's every detail exists in service of answering that question as fully, honestly and promptly as the law both requires and allows, rather than being read as a set of technical hurdles for a requester to clear before Alderbridge will engage properly with their request.

Providing data in an accessible format

Where a requester has a disability or other need affecting how they can receive information (for example, a visual impairment requiring large print, or a preference for information read aloud over the phone), the Data Protection Lead provides the response in an accessible format the requester can actually use, treating this as a normal, expected accommodation rather than an unusual, burdensome special request.

Escalation where a requester disputes the completeness of a response

Where a requester believes information has been withheld or missed, the Data Protection Lead reviews the original search scope and methodology with them, explaining what was searched and why, and conducts a further targeted search if a genuinely plausible gap is identified, rather than simply asserting the original response was complete without re-examining the specific concern raised.

Right to complain to the ICO

Every SAR response reminds the requester of their right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office if they remain dissatisfied, presented as a genuine, normal option rather than something Alderbridge is reluctant to mention, since a requester who feels this route is being hidden from them is likely to trust the substantive response far less, regardless of how genuinely thorough it actually was.

Closing note

A SAR handled well leaves the requester with a clear, complete and genuinely comprehensible answer to a simple, entirely reasonable question, delivered on time and in a tone that reflects respect for the right they are exercising, and that outcome, not merely technical compliance with the one-month clock, is what this procedure is ultimately trying to achieve on every single occasion it is used.

Data protection impact assessments

A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is completed before Alderbridge introduces any new
technology or process likely to result in a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms — for example, a
new type of monitoring sensor in a resident's room, or a new AI-assisted rostering tool that processes staff
personal data in a novel way. The DPIA is led by the Data Protection Lead, involves genuine consultation
with the people supported or staff who would be affected wherever practicable rather than being
completed as a desk exercise alone, and its outcome — including any mitigation adopted or, in a small
number of cases, a decision not to proceed with the proposal at all — is recorded and retained as
evidence that the risk was actually considered before roll-out, not afterward.

Relationship with consent-based marketing

Where Alderbridge occasionally sends a newsletter or event invitation to family members who have opted
in, that processing is kept entirely separate from care-related communication: consent is recorded
specifically for the marketing purpose, can be withdrawn at any time through a clearly signposted method
in every communication sent, and withdrawing that consent never affects, or is ever perceived to affect,
the standard of care a resident receives — a boundary Alderbridge treats as absolute precisely because of
the vulnerability of the relationship involved.

Third-party requests for information

A request for personal data from a party other than the data subject themselves — a solicitor, an insurer,
the police, or another care provider a resident is transferring to — is never actioned on the strength of the
request alone. The Data Protection Lead confirms the requester's legal basis and identity first, and where
the request comes from the police, confirms whether it is made under a specific statutory
information-sharing power before any data is released, recording that confirmation in writing regardless of
how routine or urgent the request appears to be, since urgency is never itself a substitute for lawful basis.

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains safe use of a printer and scanner at an Alderbridge site. It applies to every staff member using shared print and scan equipment.

Policy statement

A document containing resident data is printed using secure PIN release, and scan-to-email now also requires PIN authentication before sending, a new extension introduced in this version, with a printer or scanner reaching end of life now requiring a mandatory data wipe.

Definitions

**Shared printer or scanner** equipment used by multiple staff. **Secure PIN release** the mandatory printing method requiring a personal PIN before a document prints. **Scan-to-email PIN authentication** the new requirement, introduced in this version, extending PIN authentication to the scan-to-email function. **End-of-life data wipe** the new mandatory step, introduced in this version, wiping a printer or scanner's internal storage before disposal or return.

1. Print any document containing resident data using secure PIN release.
2. Authenticate with your PIN before using the scan-to-email function; this is a new requirement introduced in this version, extending the previous print-only PIN control.
3. Scan a document to the correct, intended recipient only, double-checking the destination before sending.
4. Shred a printed draft or misprint containing resident data.
5. IT completes a data wipe of a printer or scanner's internal storage before it is disposed of, returned to a leasing company, or repurposed; this is a new mandatory step introduced in this version.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

Visiting Arrangements Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how family and friends visit a resident at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every site and every visitor other than a contractor, who is covered separately by the Contractor Management Policy.

Policy statement

Open, flexible visiting is supported as a resident's normal right, restricted only where a specific, documented safeguarding or infection control reason genuinely requires it, never as a blanket default.

Definitions

**Open visiting** the standard approach of welcoming a visitor at a time that suits the resident and visitor, without a fixed visiting-hours restriction. **Restricted visiting** a documented, resident-specific limitation applied only for a genuine safeguarding or infection control reason. **Sign-in** the reception record every visitor completes on arrival.

Roles and responsibilities

**Reception or the shift lead** greets a visitor, ensures they sign in, and directs them appropriately. **The registered manager** decides and documents any restricted visiting arrangement for a specific resident. **Care staff** raise a concern about a visitor's conduct promptly rather than managing it informally themselves.

Welcome a visitor at a time that suits the resident, without requiring advance notice for a routine visit.

Ensure every visitor signs in at reception, supporting an accurate record of who is on site.

Apply a restricted visiting arrangement only where the registered manager has documented a specific safeguarding or infection control reason for that resident.

Support a resident to decline a visit from anyone they do not wish to see, including a family member, without requiring them to justify this wish.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a visitor's conduct raises an immediate concern, such as appearing intoxicated or behaving aggressively, staff may ask them to leave that day pending a documented review, without this constituting a standing restricted visiting arrangement unless the registered manager subsequently decides one is needed.

Purpose and scope

relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its

Definitions

**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any

unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from

sparse_candidates.chunk_text:
Statement. Race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation are each protected in recruitment, employment and care delivery alike, and a resident's own view is never used to justify discriminatory treatment of a member of staff on any of these grounds, even where the resident's view reflects a genuinely held but discriminatory personal belief.

Handling a resident's discriminatory request in practice

Where a resident expresses a discriminatory preference about who provides their care, the registered manager discusses this sensitively with the resident directly, explaining Alderbridge's position, and considers whether the underlying need behind the request (for example, a genuine same-sex-carer preference for intimate personal care, which is a legitimate dignity consideration) can be met without discriminating against staff on a protected characteristic; where the request is simply discriminatory with no such legitimate underlying need, it is not accommodated, and the conversation with the resident and, where relevant, their family is recorded in their care plan so the position is consistent across every shift and every member of staff involved in their care.

Appendix: reasonable adjustments in recruitment

This appendix illustrates common reasonable adjustments made during Alderbridge recruitment, for hiring managers unfamiliar with the range of what might be requested. A candidate with dyslexia may be given extra time for a written exercise, or the option to complete it verbally instead, agreed in advance rather than raised as a surprise on the day. A candidate with a hearing impairment may be offered a British Sign Language interpreter or a written transcript of interview questions in advance. A candidate with a mobility impairment is offered step-free interview access at every Alderbridge site, confirmed in the invitation itself rather than left for the candidate to ask about. A candidate managing a mental health condition may request a shorter interview with scheduled breaks. None of these adjustments are treated as exceptional accommodations requiring special justification once genuinely requested — hiring managers are trained to expect and normalise such requests as an ordinary part of running a fair process.

*Supersedes the version effective 1 March 2024. Withdraws the bring-your-own-device allowance for roles accessing resident health records; those roles now require a company-issued device only.*

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages mobile devices, including phones and tablets used to access resident records or care systems. It applies to every company-issued device and, for roles not accessing resident health records, every personal device approved for work use.

Policy statement

A mobile device that can access resident information is managed to the same security standard as an office computer, and for roles accessing resident health records specifically, only a company-issued device is now used, so that resident data remains protected wherever it is accessed from.

Definitions

**Company-issued device** a phone or tablet provided by Alderbridge and enrolled in the mobile device management system before use. **Approved personal device** a staff member's own phone or tablet, approved by IT and enrolled in the same system, now used only under a bring-your-own-device arrangement for roles not accessing resident health records. **Enrolment** the process of registering a device in the mobile device management system, applying required security settings before it can access any Alderbridge system.

Roles and responsibilities

**IT** enrols every device, company-issued or approved personal, before it is permitted to access any Alderbridge system, confirms which roles require a company-issued device under this version, and can remotely wipe a lost or stolen device. **The device user** reports a lost or stolen device to IT immediately and never disables the security settings the enrolment process applies. **The registered manager** approves which staff roles require mobile access to resident systems at their site and confirms which of those roles now require a company-issued device.

Frequently asked questions (continued)

**What if two residents have almost identical names?** The photograph on the MAR chart, not the name alone, is the primary identity check in this situation, and any site with this risk flags it explicitly on both residents' care plans so incoming and agency staff are alerted before their first round. **Can a dose be pre-poured for a resident who is out at an appointment?** No — medication is never pre-poured for later administration by a different person or at a significantly different time; if a resident is out at the scheduled time, the dose is given on their return within a reasonable window, recorded accordingly, or omitted with the reason recorded if the window has genuinely passed. **What if the MAR chart itself is damaged or illegible?** A new MAR chart is transcribed by two staff who check every entry against the original before the original is retained as a reference copy, never against memory alone. **Who checks that a locum GP's handwritten prescription matches what's already on the MAR chart?** The senior carer on duty at the time the prescription is received checks it against the current MAR chart and queries any discrepancy with the surgery before adding it, rather than assuming a handwritten instruction automatically overrides what is already recorded.

Induction and shadowing before competency assessment

A new starter joining a care-facing role does not administer medication, even under direct supervision, until they have completed the classroom-based medication training module described in the Mandatory Training Matrix. Following that module, they shadow an experienced, competency-assessed colleague for a minimum of three full rounds before beginning their own observed competency assessment, and the shadowing colleague records specific observations (not merely attendance) that feed into the eventual competency sign-off rather than being treated as a separate, disconnected step.

Providing data in an accessible format

Where a requester has a disability or other need affecting how they can receive information (for example, a visual impairment requiring large print, or a preference for information read aloud over the phone), the Data Protection Lead provides the response in an accessible format the requester can actually use, treating this as a normal, expected accommodation rather than an unusual, burdensome special request.

Escalation where a requester disputes the completeness of a response

Right to complain to the ICO

Extended frequently asked questions

**What if a resident is prescribed a controlled drug for the first time and no cabinet space is available?**
The registered manager arranges additional secure storage the same day, following the same
bolted-cabinet standard, rather than storing the new medication in a general medication trolley even
temporarily. **Can a controlled drug be transported between sites (for example, if a resident moves)?**
Yes, but only in a locked, tamper-evident container, transported by two staff, with the transfer itself
recorded in both the losing and receiving site's registers on the same day. **Who checks the denaturing kit
itself hasn't expired?** The senior carer or nurse completing the monthly medication room check includes
the denaturing kit's own expiry date as a standing item, replacing it before it expires rather than
discovering the problem only when a disposal is actually needed. **Is a discrepancy that is immediately
traced to a documented, witnessed early administration (given slightly ahead of schedule for a legitimate
clinical reason) still treated as a full discrepancy investigation?** No — where the two-person witnessing
and same-session signing standard was fully met at the time, and the register itself already explains the
timing, this is a normal variation rather than a discrepancy requiring the escalation process above; the
distinction is whether the paperwork already tells the full story, not whether the timing was unusual.

Handover between shifts

At every shift handover involving controlled drugs, the outgoing and incoming senior carers or nurses
jointly recount the physical stock of each controlled drug against the register together, signing the
handover section of the register regardless of whether an administration occurred during the preceding
shift, so that responsibility for the cabinet's contents is never ambiguous about which shift held it at any
given time, and so that a discrepancy is always narrowed down to a specific, identifiable shift rather than
an unattributable multi-day window.

Where a site's activities programme includes a trip or outing, a resident is supported to join if they wish, with staff arranging appropriate transport and any additional support a resident needs.

sparse_candidates.chunk_text:
**Can a resident's family request a specific technique they've seen work well elsewhere?** Their input is welcomed and discussed with the reviewing professional as part of the MHRA review, but the technique actually used is always the one the current, professionally reviewed MHRA specifies, not one adopted informally on a family's request alone.

Reviewing manual handling incidents for equipment versus technique cause

Where a manual handling incident occurs, the subsequent review distinguishes explicitly between an equipment failure (which triggers an immediate equipment check across the site, not only the specific item involved) and a technique deviation (which triggers a refresher and, where appropriate, a wider look at whether the training itself needs updating), since conflating the two risks either an unaddressed equipment fault recurring or an individual being unfairly blamed for what was actually an equipment problem.

Manual handling during an emergency evacuation

The Fire Safety Policy's own PEEP arrangements take precedence during a genuine evacuation, meaning a person may be moved using whatever method their PEEP specifies for evacuation specifically, which can differ from their everyday MHRA where a faster, evacuation-specific method (for example, an evacuation sledge down a stairwell) is what the PEEP requires; staff are trained to recognise this is a deliberate, planned difference between the two documents, not a contradiction to resolve in the moment.

Closing note on culture

Alderbridge treats a member of staff raising a concern about a manual handling technique or piece of equipment as a positive contribution to safety, never as a complaint to be managed defensively, since the staff actually performing a technique every day are often the first to notice a genuine problem with it long before an audit or a formal review would otherwise catch it.

A final note on consistency across the organisation

The same MHRA format, the same equipment standard, and the same training curriculum apply across all five sites, so that a resident moving between Alderbridge homes, or a staff member covering a shift at an unfamiliar site, encounters a genuinely consistent approach rather than five subtly different local conventions that happen to share the same policy title.

assistive technology alongside checks

Where a site has assistive technology such as a bed sensor or door sensor, this supports but never replaces the scheduled check, since technology can fail or miss something a direct check would catch, and a resident's safety should never depend on a single layer of monitoring alone.

Staffing levels overnight

The registered manager sets overnight staffing levels with the checking workload specifically in mind, since a genuinely achievable 2-hour cycle for every resident depends on enough staff being on duty to complete it thoroughly rather than rushed, particularly at a site with a larger or higher-dependency resident group.

Handover between night and day shifts

The outgoing night shift briefs the incoming day shift on anything noticed during the night's checks, however minor it seemed at the time, since a small overnight observation can matter to how the day shift plans a resident's care that morning.

Closing note

A well-timed, sensitively conducted check protects a resident's safety without unnecessarily disturbing their sleep, and this procedure exists to keep that balance right every night.

SARs made in the context of active litigation or a legal claim

Where a SAR arrives after Alderbridge is already aware of a genuine, active legal claim or dispute involving the same individual, the Data Protection Lead may take legal advice on how the SAR and any litigation-specific disclosure rules interact, but this consultation does not itself justify missing the standard statutory timescale merely because litigation is also under way; a genuine, narrow legal exemption is applied only where it actually exists and is documented, not used as a general reason for caution or delay.

Resident Finances and Appointeeship Policy

Supersedes the version effective 1 March 2025. Changes the escalation contact for a financial concern
from the Alderbridge Finance Manager to the Alderbridge Safeguarding Lead, reflecting that a financial
concern is treated primarily as a safeguarding matter.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds
or acting under a financial authority on a resident's behalf.

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Following any fall, do not move the resident until a basic check for obvious injury has been completed, unless leaving them in place presents its own risk.

Contact the on-call registered manager immediately after any fall, regardless of whether an injury is apparent.

Where injury is suspected, also contact the falls lead immediately, in addition to the on-call registered manager; this dual-contact requirement is new in this version and was not required previously.

Call emergency services immediately for a suspected serious injury, such as a suspected fracture or head injury with loss of consciousness, regardless of falls lead availability.

Record every fall, including one without apparent injury, in the resident's care record and the site's falls log, noting whether the falls lead was contacted.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where the falls lead is not immediately reachable following a suspected-injury fall, the on-call registered manager proceeds with emergency services contact where warranted without waiting, and the falls lead is updated as soon as they become available, since the new dual-contact step is additive and never delays an emergency response.

Local and regional variations

Harbour View's higher proportion of residents with complex mobility needs means it holds a dedicated falls prevention equipment store, including a range of mobility aids not routinely stocked at smaller sites, and its falls lead role is filled by a permanent on-site physiotherapist given the site's larger nursing capacity.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the Incident Reporting Policy (governing the wider incident record a fall also triggers) and the CQC Notification Procedure (governing when a fall meets the notifiable serious injury threshold).

Worked example

Subject Access Request (SAR) Handling Procedure

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group responds to a subject access request (SAR) — a request from a data subject to see the personal data held about them — under the UK GDPR. It applies to any SAR received about a person supported, a current or former employee, or anyone else whose personal data Alderbridge holds.

Policy statement

Alderbridge treats a subject access request as a genuine legal right the requester is exercising, not an administrative inconvenience to be managed reluctantly, and aims to respond helpfully and within the statutory timescale in every case, escalating only where a request is genuinely complex or unclear rather than defaulting to caution as a way of buying time.

Definitions

**Subject access request (SAR)** a request by a data subject (or someone with valid authority to act for them) to see the personal data held about them. **Third-party data** personal data about someone other than the requester contained within the same record, which is redacted before disclosure unless that third party consents. **Complex request** a SAR involving a particularly large volume of data or multiple systems, extending the standard response timescale. **Valid authority** the legal basis (for example, a Lasting Power of Attorney, or the data subject's own written consent) required before Alderbridge discloses personal data to someone other than the data subject themselves.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any member of staff** receiving what might be a SAR, however informally phrased, forwards it to the Data Protection Lead the same day, rather than attempting to gather the information themselves. **The Data Protection Lead** confirms the requester's identity and any authority claimed, coordinates gathering the relevant records across every system that might hold them, and completes any necessary redaction before disclosure. **Each registered manager and HR** supports the Data Protection Lead by identifying and providing the records held at their own site or function promptly when asked.

where a resident's grandchild's details appear in a visiting log; a request made on a child's behalf by a parent is assessed for the parent's own valid authority in the same way as any other third-party request, and the Data Protection Lead seeks specialist advice where the request's scope or the family circumstances are genuinely unclear.

Verbal SARs made during a heated conversation

Where a verbal SAR is made during an otherwise heated or emotional conversation (for example, during a complaint discussion), it is still treated as a valid, timescale-triggering request, and the member of staff present notes down as much detail as they reasonably can (who, roughly what was asked, when) before forwarding it, rather than the request being lost or forgotten simply because it arose in a difficult conversational context rather than a calm, deliberate one.

Proportionate search effort for a large or long-standing record

For a data subject with a very long history at Alderbridge, the search for relevant records is still comprehensive, but the Data Protection Lead may agree a reasonable, transparent approach with the requester about how older or less central material (for example, historic rota records mentioning them only incidentally) is handled, rather than treating every search as requiring literally infinite effort regardless of the genuine relevance of what might be found, provided this is discussed openly with the requester rather than decided unilaterally to save effort.

SARs made in the context of active litigation or a legal claim

Where a SAR arrives after Alderbridge is already aware of a genuine, active legal claim or dispute involving the same individual, the Data Protection Lead may take legal advice on how the SAR and any litigation-specific disclosure rules interact, but this consultation does not itself justify missing the standard statutory timescale merely because litigation is also under way; a genuine, narrow legal exemption is applied only where it actually exists and is documented, not used as a general reason for caution or delay.

need.n1.hydrated.chunk_text:
asking a straightforward question — what do you know about me — and this procedure's every detail exists in service of answering that question as fully, honestly and promptly as the law both requires and allows, rather than being read as a set of technical hurdles for a requester to clear before Alderbridge will engage properly with their request.

Providing data in an accessible format

Where a requester has a disability or other need affecting how they can receive information (for example, a visual impairment requiring large print, or a preference for information read aloud over the phone), the Data Protection Lead provides the response in an accessible format the requester can actually use, treating this as a normal, expected accommodation rather than an unusual, burdensome special request.

Escalation where a requester disputes the completeness of a response

Where a requester believes information has been withheld or missed, the Data Protection Lead reviews the original search scope and methodology with them, explaining what was searched and why, and conducts a further targeted search if a genuinely plausible gap is identified, rather than simply asserting the original response was complete without re-examining the specific concern raised.

Right to complain to the ICO

Every SAR response reminds the requester of their right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office if they remain dissatisfied, presented as a genuine, normal option rather than something Alderbridge is reluctant to mention, since a requester who feels this route is being hidden from them is likely to trust the substantive response far less, regardless of how genuinely thorough it actually was.

Closing note

A SAR handled well leaves the requester with a clear, complete and genuinely comprehensible answer to a simple, entirely reasonable question, delivered on time and in a tone that reflects respect for the right they are exercising, and that outcome, not merely technical compliance with the one-month clock, is what this procedure is ultimately trying to achieve on every single occasion it is used.

Resident Finances and Appointeeship Policy

Supersedes the version effective 1 March 2025. Changes the escalation contact for a financial concern
from the Alderbridge Finance Manager to the Alderbridge Safeguarding Lead, reflecting that a financial
concern is treated primarily as a safeguarding matter.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds
or acting under a financial authority on a resident's behalf.

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Following any fall, do not move the resident until a basic check for obvious injury has been completed, unless leaving them in place presents its own risk.

Where injury is suspected, also contact the falls lead immediately, in addition to the on-call registered manager; this dual-contact requirement is new in this version and was not required previously.

Local and regional variations

Harbour View's higher proportion of residents with complex mobility needs means it holds a dedicated falls prevention equipment store, including a range of mobility aids not routinely stocked at smaller sites, and its falls lead role is filled by a permanent on-site physiotherapist given the site's larger nursing capacity.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the Incident Reporting Policy (governing the wider incident record a fall also triggers) and the CQC Notification Procedure (governing when a fall meets the notifiable serious injury threshold).

Subject Access Request (SAR) Handling Procedure

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group responds to a subject access request (SAR) — a request from a data subject to see the personal data held about them — under the UK GDPR. It applies to any SAR received about a person supported, a current or former employee, or anyone else whose personal data Alderbridge holds.

Policy statement

Alderbridge treats a subject access request as a genuine legal right the requester is exercising, not an administrative inconvenience to be managed reluctantly, and aims to respond helpfully and within the statutory timescale in every case, escalating only where a request is genuinely complex or unclear rather than defaulting to caution as a way of buying time.

Definitions

**Subject access request (SAR)** a request by a data subject (or someone with valid authority to act for them) to see the personal data held about them. **Third-party data** personal data about someone other than the requester contained within the same record, which is redacted before disclosure unless that third party consents. **Complex request** a SAR involving a particularly large volume of data or multiple systems, extending the standard response timescale. **Valid authority** the legal basis (for example, a Lasting Power of Attorney, or the data subject's own written consent) required before Alderbridge discloses personal data to someone other than the data subject themselves.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any member of staff** receiving what might be a SAR, however informally phrased, forwards it to the Data Protection Lead the same day, rather than attempting to gather the information themselves. **The Data Protection Lead** confirms the requester's identity and any authority claimed, coordinates gathering the relevant records across every system that might hold them, and completes any necessary redaction before disclosure. **Each registered manager and HR** supports the Data Protection Lead by identifying and providing the records held at their own site or function promptly when asked.

Verbal SARs made during a heated conversation

Where a verbal SAR is made during an otherwise heated or emotional conversation (for example, during a complaint discussion), it is still treated as a valid, timescale-triggering request, and the member of staff present notes down as much detail as they reasonably can (who, roughly what was asked, when) before forwarding it, rather than the request being lost or forgotten simply because it arose in a difficult conversational context rather than a calm, deliberate one.

SARs made in the context of active litigation or a legal claim

Where a SAR arrives after Alderbridge is already aware of a genuine, active legal claim or dispute involving the same individual, the Data Protection Lead may take legal advice on how the SAR and any litigation-specific disclosure rules interact, but this consultation does not itself justify missing the standard statutory timescale merely because litigation is also under way; a genuine, narrow legal exemption is applied only where it actually exists and is documented, not used as a general reason for caution or delay.

Beyond simple timescale compliance, the Data Protection Lead periodically reviews whether SAR responses have actually been experienced as helpful and complete by checking back informally with a sample of past requesters, since a response that is technically compliant but left the requester confused or still searching for the specific information they wanted has not fully achieved this procedure's own underlying purpose, whatever the compliance statistics might otherwise suggest.

Final note on the spirit of this procedure

A SAR is, at its heart, someone asking a straightforward question — what do you know about me — and this procedure's every detail exists in service of answering that question as fully, honestly and promptly as the law both requires and allows, rather than being read as a set of technical hurdles for a requester to clear before Alderbridge will engage properly with their request.

Extended frequently asked questions

Redacting third-party data is not simply blacking out a name; the Data Protection Lead considers whether the surrounding context would still make the third party identifiable even with their name removed (for example, 'the resident in the next room' in a small care home), and redacts or generalises accordingly, since a technically redacted but still practically identifying disclosure does not meet this procedure's own standard.

Where a SAR appears to be made in the context of a separate dispute (for example, a family disagreement, or an ongoing complaint), it is still handled exactly as any other SAR would be, in full and within the same timescale, since the requester's motivation for exercising their legal right does not change the right itself or Alderbridge's obligation to respond to it properly.

Lawful basis for key processing activities

Care record processing relies primarily on the lawful basis of vital interests and the performance of a task
carried out in the substantial public interest for special category health data, alongside the person's own
consent where they are able to give it meaningfully. Employment record processing relies on the
performance of the employment contract and compliance with legal obligations. CCTV footage relies on
legitimate interests in the safety and security of people supported, staff and visitors, as set out in the CCTV
Policy. Marketing communications, where they occur at all, rely on explicit consent, never legitimate
interests, and that consent can be withdrawn at any time.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Personal data may be shared without the data subject's consent, or even without their knowledge in a
genuine emergency, where doing so is necessary to protect someone's vital interests — for example,
sharing a resident's allergy information with a paramedic during a medical emergency — but this exception
is used narrowly, for the specific emergency at hand, never as a general licence to share more broadly.

Complaints involving multiple Alderbridge sites or services

Where a complaint concerns events at more than one site — for example, a resident who transferred between two Alderbridge homes — the Quality Lead coordinates a single, joined-up investigation and response rather than each site investigating its own portion separately and the complainant receiving two disconnected replies.

Appendix: what a good complaint response looks like

This appendix sets out, for anyone drafting a complaint response, the standard every response is expected to meet, expanding on the Timescales and roles described above. A good response addresses every specific point the complainant actually raised, not a general restatement of Alderbridge's own procedures; uses plain, warm language rather than defensive or overly formal wording; acknowledges clearly and specifically anything that did go wrong, without minimising it, alongside anything that was found to have gone right; explains what has changed, or will change, as a direct result of the investigation, not only what the outcome for this specific complainant was; and offers a genuine, named point of contact for any further question, rather than closing the matter down. A response that meets the letter of the 20-working-day timescale but fails this substantive standard is returned by the Quality Lead for revision before it is sent, since the timescale and the substance are both required, not one traded off against the other.

Learning from complaints across the sector

Beyond its own complaint data, the Quality Lead periodically reviews published CQC and Ombudsman findings from the wider care sector for recurring themes (for example, a national pattern of complaints about care transitions between hospital and care home), and considers proactively whether Alderbridge's own practice in that area needs review, rather than waiting for a similar complaint to be raised internally before addressing a risk that has already been identified as common elsewhere.

Complaints made about a specific member of staff

Where a complaint names or clearly identifies a specific member of staff, that staff member is told the substance of the complaint and given a fair opportunity to give their own account before the investigation concludes, and the outcome — whether the complaint is upheld, partially upheld, or not upheld — is communicated to that staff member directly, separately from the response sent to the complainant, so the two communications can each be pitched appropriately to their different audience and purpose.

This is immediately recognised as a serious complaint, and the on-call structure ensures the Quality Lead is informed within the new 2-hour window, a noticeably faster standard than the previous version's 4-hour allowance for exactly this kind of out-of-hours scenario.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was the escalation window shortened?** A review found that a 4-hour window occasionally meant the Quality Lead learned of a serious complaint later than ideal for coordinating an immediate response; 2 hours closes that gap. **Does a serious complaint also need to go through the routine complaints process?** Yes, the urgent escalation runs alongside, not instead of, the normal complaints process.

Closing note

A fast, reliable escalation route for a serious complaint protects a resident and reassures a worried family, and the tightened window in this version exists to make that speed even more dependable.

Extended worked example: a lost unencrypted device

A worked example illustrates a more serious breach. A community support worker's personal, unencrypted
phone, on which the lone-worker app was installed alongside some informal notes about client visits, is
lost during a shift. This is reported immediately, and the Data Protection Lead assesses it as notifiable

within 72 hours, and, since the risk to the specific clients whose information may have been exposed is
genuinely elevated, notifies those individuals directly with practical guidance; separately, this incident

personal device was being used to store any client information at all, closing the underlying practice gap
rather than treating the incident as resolved once the notification obligations are met.

internally as any external communication would be, since a culture of internal minimisation about a
breach's true severity undermines the organisation's ability to learn from it, even where the external, legally
required notifications are handled correctly.

Where a full investigation will genuinely take some time, the Data Protection Lead puts interim measures
in place immediately where a plausible, proportionate one exists — for example, temporarily suspending a
specific system's remote access pending confirmation of how a credential was compromised — rather
than waiting for the complete investigation to conclude before taking any protective action at all.

Complaints Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how anyone — a person supported, a family member, a representative, or a member of the public — can raise a complaint about Alderbridge Care Group, and how that complaint is handled fairly, promptly and openly. It applies to every site and every service Alderbridge provides.

Policy statement

Alderbridge treats a complaint as valuable information about how care is actually experienced, not as a criticism to be minimised or managed away. Every complaint is looked into properly, regardless of how it is raised or how minor it might initially appear.

Definitions

**Complaint** an expression of dissatisfaction, however made, about the standard of service, actions or lack of action by Alderbridge or its staff. **Compliment** positive feedback, recorded alongside complaints for a balanced picture, per the Compliments and Feedback Log. **Duty of candour** the legal and professional duty to be open and honest when something has gone wrong and caused harm, governed in more detail by the Duty of Candour Guidance.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any member of staff** receiving a complaint, however informally, notes it and passes it to the registered manager the same day. **The registered manager** investigates and responds to most complaints at site level. **The Alderbridge Quality Lead** handles any complaint escalated beyond site level, or any complaint of particular seriousness regardless of the stage it is at.

A complaint may be made verbally to any member of staff, in writing, by phone, or in person to the registered manager — no specific format is required for a complaint to be valid.

The complaint is acknowledged within 3 working days, in writing, confirming who is handling it and the expected timescale.

The registered manager (or Quality Lead, for an escalated complaint) investigates, which may include speaking to staff, reviewing records, and speaking again with the complainant to clarify what outcome they are looking for.

**The Data Protection Lead** is Alderbridge's own nominated individual accountable for data protection

Personal Data Breach Procedure

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group responds to a suspected or confirmed personal data
breach, under the UK GDPR's own breach-notification requirements. It applies to any incident involving
personal data — a lost device, a misdirected email, unauthorised access, or a genuine cyber incident —
regardless of how minor it initially appears.

Policy statement

Alderbridge treats a fast, honest internal report of a suspected breach as far more valuable than a delayed,
polished one, and this procedure is deliberately built around a very short internal reporting window, since
the regulatory 72-hour clock for a notifiable breach starts running from when Alderbridge becomes aware
of it, not from when the investigation concludes.

Definitions

**Personal data breach** a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss,
alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data. **Notifiable breach** a breach likely to
result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, requiring notification to the Information Commissioner's
Office within 72 hours of Alderbridge becoming aware of it. **High-risk breach** a breach likely to result in
a high risk to individuals, additionally requiring the affected individuals themselves to be notified without
undue delay. **Containment** the immediate action taken to stop a breach continuing or worsening (for

Appendix: the 72-hour clock at a glance

For quick reference: the clock starts when Alderbridge becomes aware of the breach, not when the
investigation concludes; internal reporting within 1 hour of discovery gives the Data Protection Lead the
maximum possible time within that window to investigate properly and, where required, notify the ICO with
a genuinely complete, accurate assessment rather than a rushed, incomplete one submitted only to beat
the deadline.

Breaches involving a third-party data processor

Where a breach occurs at a third-party data processor holding Alderbridge data (for example, a payroll
provider), the processor's own contractual obligation to notify Alderbridge without undue delay is relied on,
but the Data Protection Lead also proactively checks in with key processors periodically, since the 72-hour
clock for Alderbridge's own notification obligation still runs from when Alderbridge itself becomes aware,
which can be later than when the processor's own breach actually occurred if the processor is slow to tell
Alderbridge.

Extended frequently asked questions

**What if the breach involves a former employee's data rather than a current one?** The same procedure
applies in full; a former employee's data remains protected personal data for as long as Alderbridge holds
it. **Can a breach be assessed as low risk simply because the recipient is another Alderbridge employee
rather than an external party?** No — an internal misdirection can still be a genuine breach, particularly for
special category health data, and is assessed on the actual risk to the individual concerned, not assumed
low risk purely because it stayed within the organisation. **Is a physical break-in and theft of paper records
treated the same as a digital breach?** Yes — the same assessment and notification process applies
regardless of whether the compromised data was digital or physical.

Policy statement

own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any

the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

Where a SAR arrives after Alderbridge is already aware of a genuine, active legal claim or dispute involving the same individual, the Data Protection Lead may take legal advice on how the SAR and any litigation-specific disclosure rules interact, but this consultation does not itself justify missing the standard statutory timescale merely because litigation is also under way; a genuine, narrow legal exemption is applied only where it actually exists and is documented, not used as a general reason for caution or delay.

Statement. Race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation are each protected in recruitment, employment and care delivery alike, and a resident's own view is never used to justify discriminatory treatment of a member of staff on any of these grounds, even where the resident's view reflects a genuinely held but discriminatory personal belief.

Handling a resident's discriminatory request in practice

Where a resident expresses a discriminatory preference about who provides their care, the registered manager discusses this sensitively with the resident directly, explaining Alderbridge's position, and considers whether the underlying need behind the request (for example, a genuine same-sex-carer preference for intimate personal care, which is a legitimate dignity consideration) can be met without discriminating against staff on a protected characteristic; where the request is simply discriminatory with no such legitimate underlying need, it is not accommodated, and the conversation with the resident and, where relevant, their family is recorded in their care plan so the position is consistent across every shift and every member of staff involved in their care.

Appendix: reasonable adjustments in recruitment

This appendix illustrates common reasonable adjustments made during Alderbridge recruitment, for hiring managers unfamiliar with the range of what might be requested. A candidate with dyslexia may be given extra time for a written exercise, or the option to complete it verbally instead, agreed in advance rather than raised as a surprise on the day. A candidate with a hearing impairment may be offered a British Sign Language interpreter or a written transcript of interview questions in advance. A candidate with a mobility impairment is offered step-free interview access at every Alderbridge site, confirmed in the invitation itself rather than left for the candidate to ask about. A candidate managing a mental health condition may request a shorter interview with scheduled breaks. None of these adjustments are treated as exceptional accommodations requiring special justification once genuinely requested — hiring managers are trained to expect and normalise such requests as an ordinary part of running a fair process.

Mobile Device Management Policy

*Supersedes the version effective 1 March 2024. Withdraws the bring-your-own-device allowance for roles accessing resident health records; those roles now require a company-issued device only.*

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages mobile devices, including phones and tablets used to access resident records or care systems. It applies to every company-issued device and, for roles not accessing resident health records, every personal device approved for work use.

Policy statement

A mobile device that can access resident information is managed to the same security standard as an office computer, and for roles accessing resident health records specifically, only a company-issued device is now used, so that resident data remains protected wherever it is accessed from.

Definitions

**Company-issued device** a phone or tablet provided by Alderbridge and enrolled in the mobile device management system before use. **Approved personal device** a staff member's own phone or tablet, approved by IT and enrolled in the same system, now used only under a bring-your-own-device arrangement for roles not accessing resident health records. **Enrolment** the process of registering a device in the mobile device management system, applying required security settings before it can access any Alderbridge system.

Roles and responsibilities

**IT** enrols every device, company-issued or approved personal, before it is permitted to access any Alderbridge system, confirms which roles require a company-issued device under this version, and can remotely wipe a lost or stolen device. **The device user** reports a lost or stolen device to IT immediately and never disables the security settings the enrolment process applies. **The registered manager** approves which staff roles require mobile access to resident systems at their site and confirms which of those roles now require a company-issued device.

A worked example illustrates a genuinely difficult overlap. A resident's family member submits a SAR while a safeguarding investigation involving that same family member is ongoing. Quality checking a response before it is sent

Before any SAR response is sent, a second person (not the person who prepared it) reviews it specifically for redaction completeness and factual accuracy, since a redaction mistake in a SAR response is itself a personal data breach under the Personal Data Breach Procedure, and this second check is a control specifically designed to prevent that particular failure mode.

Requests about a child in a family member's care

Occasionally a SAR-like request concerns a child rather than an adult data subject — for example, where a resident's grandchild's details appear in a visiting log; a request made on a child's behalf by a parent is assessed for the parent's own valid authority in the same way as any other third-party request, and the Data Protection Lead seeks specialist advice where the request's scope or the family circumstances are genuinely unclear.

**What if two residents have almost identical names?** The photograph on the MAR chart, not the name alone, is the primary identity check in this situation, and any site with this risk flags it explicitly on both residents' care plans so incoming and agency staff are alerted before their first round. **Can a dose be pre-poured for a resident who is out at an appointment?** No — medication is never pre-poured for later administration by a different person or at a significantly different time; if a resident is out at the scheduled time, the dose is given on their return within a reasonable window, recorded accordingly, or omitted with the reason recorded if the window has genuinely passed. **What if the MAR chart itself is damaged or illegible?** A new MAR chart is transcribed by two staff who check every entry against the original before the original is retained as a reference copy, never against memory alone. **Who checks that a locum GP's handwritten prescription matches what's already on the MAR chart?** The senior carer on duty at the time the prescription is received checks it against the current MAR chart and queries any discrepancy with the surgery before adding it, rather than assuming a handwritten instruction automatically overrides what is already recorded.

Supersedes the version effective 1 March 2025. Adds the falls lead nurse or therapist as a mandatory escalation contact, alongside the on-call registered manager, for any fall with suspected injury.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group assesses falls risk and responds when a resident falls. It applies to every resident, with particular attention to a resident identified as being at higher risk.

Policy statement

Falls prevention balances a resident's right to move around freely with a proportionate response to their individual risk, since an overly restrictive approach can itself cause harm by reducing a resident's mobility, confidence and independence.

Definitions

**Falls risk assessment** the structured assessment completed for every resident at admission and reviewed regularly thereafter. **Post-fall protocol** the immediate response steps followed after any fall, regardless of apparent severity. **Falls lead** the nurse or therapist now designated at each site as a mandatory escalation contact, alongside the on-call registered manager, for any fall with suspected injury.

Roles and responsibilities

**Care staff** follow the post-fall protocol immediately after any fall and contact the on-call registered manager, and now also the falls lead where injury is suspected. **The registered manager** reviews the falls risk assessment after any fall and updates the care plan accordingly. **The falls lead** provides a clinical assessment for any suspected-injury fall, a new role introduced in this version, working alongside the GP or emergency services where further escalation is needed.

Complete a falls risk assessment at admission and review it at least every three months, or sooner following any fall.

Following any fall, do not move the resident until a basic check for obvious injury has been completed, unless leaving them in place presents its own risk.

sparse_candidates.chunk_text:
**Can a resident's family request a specific technique they've seen work well elsewhere?** Their input is welcomed and discussed with the reviewing professional as part of the MHRA review, but the technique actually used is always the one the current, professionally reviewed MHRA specifies, not one adopted informally on a family's request alone.

Reviewing manual handling incidents for equipment versus technique cause

Where a manual handling incident occurs, the subsequent review distinguishes explicitly between an equipment failure (which triggers an immediate equipment check across the site, not only the specific item involved) and a technique deviation (which triggers a refresher and, where appropriate, a wider look at whether the training itself needs updating), since conflating the two risks either an unaddressed equipment fault recurring or an individual being unfairly blamed for what was actually an equipment problem.

Manual handling during an emergency evacuation

The Fire Safety Policy's own PEEP arrangements take precedence during a genuine evacuation, meaning a person may be moved using whatever method their PEEP specifies for evacuation specifically, which can differ from their everyday MHRA where a faster, evacuation-specific method (for example, an evacuation sledge down a stairwell) is what the PEEP requires; staff are trained to recognise this is a deliberate, planned difference between the two documents, not a contradiction to resolve in the moment.

Closing note on culture

Alderbridge treats a member of staff raising a concern about a manual handling technique or piece of equipment as a positive contribution to safety, never as a complaint to be managed defensively, since the staff actually performing a technique every day are often the first to notice a genuine problem with it long before an audit or a formal review would otherwise catch it.

A final note on consistency across the organisation

The same MHRA format, the same equipment standard, and the same training curriculum apply across all five sites, so that a resident moving between Alderbridge homes, or a staff member covering a shift at an unfamiliar site, encounters a genuinely consistent approach rather than five subtly different local conventions that happen to share the same policy title.

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Wherever a resident is able to participate, their own wishes and views are sought and given real weight throughout a safeguarding process, not merely noted as a formality; this is especially central to a self-neglect situation, where the resident's own account of their choices and priorities is the starting point for any supportive response.

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Where a resident's safeguarding history involves a local authority area outside where their current Alderbridge site sits, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead liaises with the originating authority to ensure relevant history transfers appropriately, using the multi-agency information sharing principles this version formalises.

Learning from a serious case review

Where Alderbridge is involved in, or a sector-wide serious case review identifies a lesson relevant to, a serious safeguarding failure, the Safeguarding Lead ensures that lesson is considered against this overarching policy and its suite, with any resulting change tracked and communicated to staff.

Supporting a staff member involved in a difficult safeguarding case

A staff member closely involved in a distressing safeguarding case, whether as the person who raised the concern or as part of the response, is offered support similar to that available following a resident's death, recognising that safeguarding work, including a self-neglect case that can be particularly difficult to sit with, is emotionally demanding even when handled well.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

Family involvement and support

After death
